name: Diffusion coefficient

summary: Give the Diffusion coefficient calculator the major axis, the friction coefficient, the friction coefficient (ξ) and the diffusion coefficient and it returns absolute temperature (T). That makes it useful for a bench calculation involving amounts, concentrations or reaction ratios. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Diffusion coefficient calculator work?
sections.html:
The Diffusion coefficient calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports absolute temperature (T) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the shape); then you type in the major axis (a), the friction coefficient (ξ), the friction coefficient (ξ) (2) and the diffusion coefficient (D).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Diffusion coefficient calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Absolute temperature (T)=diffusion coefficient (D) × friction coefficient (ξ) ÷ boltzmann's constant
Diffusion coefficient (D)=boltzmann's constant × absolute temperature (T) ÷ friction coefficient (ξ)
Solvent viscosity (η)=(1 ÷ 6) × friction coefficient (ξ) ÷ (PI × radius (a))
Solvent viscosity (η)=(1 ÷ 16) × friction coefficient (ξ) ÷ radius (a)
Solvent viscosity (η)=(3 ÷ 32) × friction coefficient (ξ) ÷ radius (a)
Solvent viscosity (η)=(1 ÷ 12) × friction coefficient (ξ) ÷ radius (a)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Heat capacity, opening in joules per kelvin
  • Temperature, opening in kelvins
  • Length, opening in nanometers
  • Length, opening in nanometers
  • Length, opening in nanometers
  • Friction coefficient, opening in seconds per kilogram
  • Friction coefficient, opening in seconds per kilogram
  • Friction coefficient, opening in seconds per kilogram

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Diffusion coefficient calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Working through a stoichiometry problem
  • Converting between the units a protocol and your bench equipment use
  • Preparing a solution and checking the numbers first
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the major axis, the friction coefficient and the friction coefficient (ξ) — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Diffusion coefficient calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns absolute temperature (T), derived from the major axis, the friction coefficient and the friction coefficient (ξ). Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Diffusion coefficient calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the major axis, the friction coefficient, the friction coefficient (ξ) and the diffusion coefficient, which is 10 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter boltzmann's constant in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Boltzmann's constant opens in joules per kelvin and the chip beside it offers 9 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Diffusion coefficient calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
